utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you be kind enough to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mr. Matthias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Andres Vatter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. After this delay which has again been caused by technical reasons, the Chamber will begin the hearing by greeting all those presents, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence attorneys, the accused, and all the staff of this courtroom. Before bringing in the witness, I'm going to ask the Registrar for us to go into closed session because the Chamber is going to render an oral decision.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the testimony of this witness, I wish to remind you that during the examination-in-chief, the Prosecution used 87 minutes. Therefore, the Defence will have two hours and 15 minutes at their disposal for the cross-examination. So theoretically, we will have time to have the cross-examination by the Defence, and for the rest of the time, if necessary, the Judges will be able to ask questions. In order to avoid wasting time, I'm going to ask Madam Usher to go and fetch our witness who is waiting. And I will immediately give the floor to Mr. Bourgon, who is already set to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Let me first check that you can hear my words in your headset properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please take a seat. As you know, the examination-in-chief has already taken place. We interrupted your testimony in order to allow the Defence to become acquainted with certain documents so as to be able to start their cross-examination. As the Defence is now able to start its cross-examination, without further ado, I'm going to give them the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me begin, sir, by acknowledging the fact that we have had the opportunity to meet when you were first here back in April. And I would like to take this opportunity to thank you for taking the time to meet with the Defence team of General Hadzihasanovic. I did introduce me -- I did introduce myself last time, but for the purpose of the transcript, let me introduce the people I am with this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. morning. I'm accompanied this morning by Ms. Edina Residovic, and by Mr. Alexis Demirdjian, and my name is Stephane Bourgon. And together, we represent General Hadzihasanovic. Once again, sir, I would like to apologise for the fact that you had to come back, of course, twice. But I take it that you understand the issue that those documents that we were looking for, and I also take this opportunity to acknowledge the fact that your own personal intervention in making us get these documents was instrumental, and I wish to thank you for this. Sir, before we begin, I would like to repeat what I said to you when we first met back in April. And at that time, I mentioned to you that in representing General Hadzihasanovic in this trial, we thought that this trial focussed on the exercise of command. In this respect, we hope to draw upon your expertise and your vast experience so that all of us here in the courtroom better understand the military profession. When you first appeared before the Trial Chamber, and that was on the 6th of April, your military background and experience was highlighted by the questions posed to you by the Prosecution. I don't intend to repeat those questions. Nevertheless, there is one topic I would like to cover with you this morning, and that is the Royal Marines. I understand that after 37 years of military service, you ended up as lieutenant general, a three-star general, and that you commanded the Royal Marines. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, many people, whether inside this courtroom or outside this courtroom, have heard about the Royal Marines, but I think very few know what the Royal Marines are about. Can you explain for the Trial Chamber what are the Royal Marines and what kind of challenges you met while commanding the Royal Marines.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, putting it as briefly as possible, the Royal Marines are the infantry of the naval service. We come under the naval service, not under the army. And the primary role of the Royal Marines is the projection of land power from sea on to land in a hostile or potentially hostile environment, particularly when there is no access to beaches, ports, or airfields. I suppose the -- one of the best examples of this in recent years was the operation to retake the Falkland Islands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself, sir, involved in the operations in the Falkland Islands? Were you still a serving member at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my eternal regret, I was not involved in the Falkland Islands. I was in our ministry of defence. It just so happened I took over the brigade a few months later, and therefore happened to be the only one in the whole brigade who had not been in the Falkland Islands. That is a lasting problem to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in terms of the -- when we talk about the Royal Marines, how big an organisation are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about some 7.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the Royal Marines is somehow referred to as the elite forces within the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We like to consider ourselves elite forces. There are, of course, others who consider themselves elite forces, but we certainly do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that if there are serious commissions or combat missions to be accomplished by the United Kingdom, the first unit that comes to mind would be the Royal Marines?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we are talking about a commanding officer, and looking at your background at various levels into the Royal Marines, I take it that you have faced a number of daunting challenges in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that being a commander, especially of an operational force in an operational situation, is not only a calling, but that it is also one of the most difficult professions one can ever exercise?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I would agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that one example of this when you are a commander of an operational force, one of those possible challenges to illustrate would be that you may be ordering your men into battle knowing that their chances of coming back alive would be slim?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't happen regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this respect, sir, would you agree with me that for anyone to be able to properly assess the work of a commanding officer in an operational situation, this could only be done by taking stock of the prevailing circumstances at the time and by trying to put one's self, even though that would be very difficult, in the shoes of the commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I would agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to your specific mission in Bosnia, of course you were not there in your capacity as a general. I understand that in mid-June 1993, you first travelled to Bosnia through Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you came to Zenica where you stayed for approximately 10 to 14 days during which time you received training and you had the opportunity to familiarise yourself with the mission.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you did have the opportunity to familiarise yourself with the parties and the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that during this period, you had regular contact with Ambassador Thebault who is the head of the regional centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you had a chance to discuss his views of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I should make the point that I was only one of a party of about 10 or 15 monitors who had moved into Bosnia, and we were being dealt with as a whole. And therefore, Jean-Pierre Thebault was not just having conversations with me, he'd be addressing the whole new team who were then going to different parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. Now, even though there was a group, would I be right in saying that you were the only amongst this group who was going as the head of a coordinating centre, and that was Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not know that until the end of my -- end of that 10 to 14 days. None of us knew where we were going until the last two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after you left for Mostar, you became the head of the coordinating centre, and that would have been towards the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early July. Early July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during your time as head of the coordinating centre in Mostar, I take it that you stayed in contact with Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you had access to the reports in Zenica, and that you yourself forwarded your reports to the same regional centre?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also understand from some documents that I have seen that Ambassador Thebault did visit you in Mostar on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the conflict that you were involved in in Mostar, of course, not involved personally, but the conflict that was ongoing and the prevailing circumstances in Mostar, would I be right to say that this was really a conflict between the HVO on the one hand and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the other?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so, yes, with the additional factor that Mostar was being shelled regularly on a random basis by the Serbs, by the Bosnian Serb Army who were just over the mountains to the east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in some respect, we can say that the situation in Mostar was in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. some respect parallel to the situation in Central Bosnia where you were to become the head of the regional centre?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In October, you were designated as the head of the regional centre. And I understand from our conversation that on this occasion, you had quite a detailed handover with Ambassador Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on this occasion, then, you had the opportunity to discuss his views.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like, sir, to show you one document which highlights the views of Ambassador Thebault and simply to ask you if some of these views of Ambassador Thebault and simply to ask you if some of these views raised in this document were communicated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this point in time, I'd like to provide everyone in the courtroom with a series of documents that have been put into bundles in order to facilitate matters for everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, due to some mistake, the document I wish to show you at this time is not included in this collection. What I propose to do is to -- to use the ELMO that is beside you in order for you to read this document while everyone can see it in the courtroom. This is a document dated 4th of August 1993. And the subject of the document is "human rights situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, an emergency situation." And it is prepared by Jean-Pierre Thebault. If I can ask the usher, please, to take the document and to put it on the ELMO so that everyone can see the document. Sir, I would like to refer you to this document which talks about a situation as of 4 August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to point out that the parts that are highlighted were highlighted by myself when preparing for this. But unfortunately I don't have copies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Where we talk at the top of the document where we mention "this flow of thousands of people has submerged the border with Croatia." And then moving down to the next paragraph where we talk about "if those moves have been greatly prepared by the effects of the irrationally passionate Croat propaganda describing since months all Muslims as fundamentalists and Mujahedin slaughtering women and children, as well as encouraged by the decision of local HVO politicians, it is really today a tragic humanitarian situation." And I go on to read just this paragraph: "The HVO accusations of Muslim slaughtering actions are quite totally without justifications, but their resulting ethnic cleansing of the last fighting is a sad truth. It has to be recognised that BiH Army has always granted protection for the remaining Croat population before, during, and after the fighting. But the mistrust is too high, and the rumours are too strong." I stop here, sir, to ask you whether this issue of Croat propaganda of the resulting ethnic cleansing and the challenges which arise from this situation, if you had the chance to discuss this with Ambassador Thebault before taking on your duties as head of the regional centre?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have discussed this in general terms certainly. I did not discuss this specific report with him, which is written about a month after I moved down to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the situation itself concerning the Croat propaganda, is this something you are able to comment upon?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think inevitably, all sides in Bosnia indulged in propaganda. Certainly in the Mostar area, the leaders did describe the Muslims as fundamentalists, and they were very concerned that we, the Europeans, were not aware of an impending Islamic fundamentalist state in Bosnia. This was a regular theme of the Croats, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document into evidence. It was prepared by the witness's predecessor. The witness can't recognise -- identify the document because it was prepared before his time. But it's an official document and I would request that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, as far as this document is concerned, it was drafted by the Ambassador. What would your position be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only part of the document I've seen was that which was shown on the ELMO. Perhaps if I could actually see the full document, I could state our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, perhaps we could put the second page of the document on the ELMO so that everyone can see the second page. And immediately after the break, I will have copies for everyone. Perhaps we could wait to tender it into evidence until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of your responsibilities as head of the regional centre, and that first one being that both when you testified last time in April, on three occasions, you mentioned that the duties of the ECMM was first political; secondly, military; and thirdly, humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if there is a specific reason for this at the order, because it appears that this was something important that you've repeated three times, that it was first political, then military, then humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think everyone recognised that the only long-term solution to the situation in Bosnia and indeed elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia was going to be a political one. And therefore, the political side had a priority. But it was -- we were in the middle of a war, and therefore the military side was crucially important. And as I think I may have mentioned last time, in Bosnia the political and the military sides were very closely interlinked. I could talk to military leaders about politics, and to political leaders about military matters. But the reasons why they were in that order, political, military, and humanitarian, because it was considered that the political was the most important issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying, sir, that on the basis of this order of priority, that the ECMM mission was really in Bosnia to look at the big picture, especially for the benefit of foreign departments of various states?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was our job to collectively to provide all our nations, all the nations of Europe, with an as accurate a picture as we could manage of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you a new document, sir, and see if you can tell me whether this document represents both the mission of the ECMM. This is a document which was prepared by the European Community liaison officer at the Bosnia and Herzegovina command in Kiseljak. You will recognise on this document, of course, the role, focus, and main mode of action, but also that this document was prepared at the time you were the head of the regional centre in Zenica. Would you agree, looking at page 2, that this was basically the way the ECMM functioned in Bosnia, and that on page 3 is basically your own organisation of the regional centre Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I could just clarify that the date of this document, 7th of July, in fact I was not the head of the regional centre Zenica. I was in Mostar. But looking at the third page, there's a slight misunderstanding here. The 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I may just for --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the -- that is there -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the Brioni agreement which gave way to this mission?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The third page, that is the organisation of RC Zenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, after I have concluded my cross-examination, I'll be requesting that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, as far as this document is concerned, on the first page, the 7th of July 1991, that must be a mistake. It must be 1993. And I can also see that on page 2 and on page 3, these pages don't have the same type of print as page number 1. This document has certainly been put together from two sources. There's a document that was drafted at another time than pages 2 and 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If I have a look at the date, the 7th of July 1991, that was the date of an agreement that was signed that made it possible for the mission to be established. But before this mission started functioning in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it had already started functioning in Slovenia. So the date, 1991, is correct. As far as the Chamber's comments on the type, the print in the document, I'd just like to point out that this document was located on Prosecutor's electronic site. And if we have a look at the numbers at the bottom, you have pages 7249, and 7251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say is that the page that mentions the witness -- which mentions the presence of the witness in 1993 can't have been drafted in 1991. So the document you are giving us must have been put together by using a number of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to point out that if we have a look at the heading on the first page, it's a document that consists of three pages, and there was a brief that was prepared by the liaison officer. And the sources were referred to, and the situation was explained at the time. But I only wanted to facilitate the Trial Chamber's work. So if the Trial Chamber refuses to admit the document into evidence, that doesn't cause any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the document is concerned, what is the Prosecution's position? The witness has recognised this document when he examined page number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to support what my learned friend from the Defence has said, this is, in fact, a briefing document which makes reference to the Brioni agreement. The Prosecution has no objection to this document being admitted into evidence. It appears to be some type of briefing document prepared by the EC liaison officer in Kiseljak, clearly at some point in 1993, because of what the witness has testified to. It simply makes reference on the first page to the agreement establishing ECMM. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit will be DH188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look at tab number 1 of the document -- of the series of documents that have been given to you and to confirm that this was basically the organisation of the regional centre Zenica. Sorry, the big series of documents that was given to you. Under tab number 1, the first document.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on now to my first substantive topic that I wish to raise with you. And that's, of course, a follow-up to the examination-in-chief on the 6th of April. Now, in your testimony, in response to a colleague -- to a question which was asked to you by my colleague, you mentioned that you were interested in the Mujahedin issue.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said that this is why you asked what the situation was about concerning those Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked very regularly at many meetings about the Mujahedin, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in response to a question you mentioned that to you, when discussing this issue with General Hadzihasanovic and General Alagic, it was clear that both General Hadzihasanovic and his successor, Mehmet Alagic, did not like the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly the impression I received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they used to say that there were a few foreigners who were fighting well for the Bosniaks, but that there were others who clearly they would wish to have out of their area.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it appears that you had the impression or you thought that they wanted to impress on you that they had these Mujahedin under control.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be very difficult for any commander not to admit that any troops in his area were not under his control. But as I've said, I was never fully convinced that General Hadzihasanovic and General Alagic did have all these Mujahedin fully under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You beat me to my next question. Simply, that this type of general talk, when two generals who have the highest of respect for one another when they meet, it is quite normal if nothing else to appear to be in control of all the forces on the territory?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, because generals, of course, like to admit -- like to show that they are in control.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you mention in your response, you believe or you were never convinced that this was, in fact, the situation.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think, yeah, one or two incidents which -- certainly that awful incident at the end of January with the ODA, that clearly indicated to me that that was not directed by the commander of 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now. You had a conversation with General Hadzihasanovic which my colleague from the Prosecution referred to. And I'd like to refer you to tab 14 in the series of documents that you have. And on page 8 of this document, and I refer you to paragraph 10. Now, during this conversation, sir, I take it that General Hadzihasanovic was basically telling you that there were several kinds of Mujahedin; a first type which were foreigners, and that was a problem that he was trying to solve. And that he saw two solutions: Either to send them back to their countries or to integrate them. Is that a fair representation of what General Hadzihasanovic told you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I understood him to mean. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General Hadzihasanovic also referred to a second type of Mujahedins which were criminals who tried to call themselves Mujahedin because it was easier to commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he also referred to in the end of this paragraph that there were no special Mujahedin organisation and that most of these peoples were criminals who were wanted by their own country.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what he said, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the context of this conversation, and I refer you just to the paragraph just above, paragraph 9, at the end, the context of this conversation was discipline. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General Hadzihasanovic mentioned on that occasion that he had no problems with soldiers, but only with people with weapons who do not belong to the army. Do you remember General Hadzihasanovic saying that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 9 just at the end.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, absolutely. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General Hadzihasanovic, would you say from -- on the basis of this conversation, was indeed trying to solve what he considered to be a problem?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was clear to me that the Mujahedin were a problem to both Hadzihasanovic and then Alagic. And I know that they wanted to try and sort it out. As I say, I could never understand why they were ever allowed into the country in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fact that General Hadzihasanovic mentioned that he was against fundamentalism, did you recognise this in General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he used to enjoy his Slivovitz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, maybe you did not know what measures General Hadzihasanovic was taking at that time to handle this problem, or did you know what he was doing to handle the problem?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to tab number 5 in the series of documents that you have. And I would like you to take a few minutes to read this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a document that's already been admitted into evidence. It has been marked for identification, and the number is DH165.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, by looking at this letter, and I understand I'm rushing you here a bit because it's quite the... I would like to refer you to the fourth line of this document, first paragraph, where General Hadzihasanovic was referring to Arabs and Turks who have not entered the ranks of the army in spite of having been invited to, and that they are still contemplating proposals made to them by the army's chief of staff. Would you agree with me, General, that this indicates that these Arabs and Turks are not under control of the 3rd Corps but that there is something going on between someone at a higher level and the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I have not seen -- never seen this very interesting document before. But that is the clear implication of this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I refer you to the first paragraph, three lines from the bottom, where it talks about that these people wish to communicate exclusively with top officials of the army staff and not with the 3rd Corps commander. Would that indicate to you, General, that -- sorry, sir, that General Hadzihasanovic was kind of left out of the loop?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly the clear implication of this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the third paragraph, sir, to the third line where we talk about the methods of combat, but General Hadzihasanovic is expressing the view that their methods of combat is directly detrimental to the BH State and especially to the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would that be consistent with the views expressed to you by General Hadzihasanovic later on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do not recall him saying -- making this specific point, but it would be along the general lines of his suspicions of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I now refer you to one last sentence, the last paragraph, where General Hadzihasanovic is requesting your stances and opinions regarding the solution to this problem because he does not want to be held accountable. Would that be something reasonable for a commander who is faced with a problem that is beyond his control to address his superior headquarters and ask for their opinion and their help?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly absolutely understand the thrust of that last paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, we see from the last paragraph that you have four words in capital letters. And these words are "your stances and opinions." Of course, this is a translation, so we don't -- maybe these words appear a bit odd. But what I'd like to ask from you is that in a military document, for a commanding general to put some words into capital letters like this, would that be really that he is underlining a very important issue?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree. It would be unusual for a commander to put words in capital letters when he's addressing his superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you now, sir, to tab number 6 in the documents. And I'd like to go straight into the order at paragraph 1. And this is an order which is dated the 16th of June. It's three days following the first letter addressed by General Hadzihasanovic. Now, would you agree with me, sir, that what this order is telling General Hadzihasanovic is to send these groups, referring to the Arabs and the Turks, to Igman and to merge them with the SVK, meaning the supreme command independent detachment in Zuka's unit. And in case they do not accept it, to show them no hospitality and eventually to disarm them. Would you agree with me, sir, that this is basically what the solution proposed by the headquarters, to either send them away to work with an independent supreme command unit or, if they refuse, not to make any -- show them any hospitality and eventually, of course, to disarm them?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so, yes. Because "eventually" does not give a time scale, but that is clearly the meaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And eventually, even though this an order, it means that some assessment or some leeway is left to the commander to determine whether that is an appropriate solution?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the solution is there in a clear instruction. The only thing that is omitted is a time scale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you just confirm before we move to the next document that when we talk about a supreme command independent detachment, we are talking about a unit which is basically an army asset as opposed to a corps asset; that is, something that is outside of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to tab number 7. And to show you, this is a telephone conversation between General Halilovic, who was at that time chief of staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I refer you immediately to the second page at line 15. So the conversation is between General Halilovic and General Hadzihasanovic. And this is a conversation which was initiated by General Halilovic. Now, I just read you the lines 15 to 30 where it appears that General Hadzihasanovic is saying "regarding the information that we have received about those foreigners, it cannot be done that way." And General Halilovic answering: "Really?" "No way, this is my third front line." "No, no, but try, it is ordered here. Two of them have signed it. Do you understand me?" "Well, try to send one order without that second part, ordering only to send them up there." "Yeah." "I should tell them I have received a letter." "Good, but you may fax it as well." Will you agree with me, sir, that on the reading of this conversation, that what General Hadzihasanovic is actually doing on that occasion is arguing or at least highlighting the fact that the order he has received previously on the same day, the 16th of June, cannot be done in this manner and he opposes the use of force to handle the problem because he figures that this would be same as opening a third front?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that he's referring to the second sentence of the first paragraph of Delic's letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when we talk about a third front, can you, based on your knowledge of the scenario in Bosnia and Herzegovina, what General Hadzihasanovic had in mind by saying a "third front"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that not only were they fighting the Croats and the Serbs, but this would also possibly mean fighting with the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that by this letter, General Hadzihasanovic is expressing the opinion that this would not be wise, at least at this time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand this because, of course, I have never seen this before, to say that he is reluctant to disarm them because this could lead Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to fighting. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to refer you to tab number 8 in the documents, which is a new document which was sent directly to Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin on the 23rd of July. So in this document, Mr. Mahmuljin is authorised to carry out on behalf of army headquarters the necessary negotiations and arrangements with the representatives of the Mujahedin unit regarding the following issues. And that is to include the Mujahedin in the army and to use them against the Chetniks and how they could be resubordinated to the 3rd Corps command. And that this authorisation is limited to this specific issue. Will you agree, sir, that this authorisation is basically saying that the army headquarters has decided to negotiate directly with the Mujahedin, and that this Mr. Mahmuljin is authorised to do this, not on behalf of the 3rd Corps, but on behalf of the army?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you yourself, sir, know who Mr. Mahmuljin is, because you have met him later. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he took over from General Alagic as the commander of 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to move on to the next document, which is tab number 9 where we now have a proposal, and I refer you immediately to paragraph number 1. This is a document that was forwarded from 3rd Corps command to army headquarters, which proposes to organise the foreign volunteers into one detachment and to mobilise them in a collection point in a village called Mejoric, and to give a name to this unit, and to do it as quickly as possible. Would you agree, sir, that this -- by this proposal someone within 3rd Corps is proposing to establish this formation of a detachment? And I also refer you to just below the word "urgent" where it says "handwritten," it says there "organisation and mobilisation administration, I agree. Organise a temporary establishment or establish. Consider it". If you look at the second page, which is the original, this was a handwritten comment that was added. Do you agree that on this occasion, this is, of course, a follow up to the authorisation that was given. And it says there just above the word "proposal," it says: "On the basis of the authorisation 1/297 of 23 July." So that this letter is a direct follow up to the specific authorisation sent to Mr. Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Mr. Mahmuljin is proposing to organise this attachment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's certainly my understanding in reading this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the second page, the original, we see that there is a signature block where it says "commandant and Enver Hadzihasanovic," and there is no signature. Now, would you agree with me that there are many reasons why a document ends up in army headquarters without a signature?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be very unusual because even if the general was not present, it would normally be signed by his deputy. So it's unusual to have an unsigned document being forwarded in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, will you agree with me, sir, on the basis of your experience that within a headquarters, there is a specific way for authorising documents whether a document is authorised by the commander, whether a document is authorised for the commander, and whether some people use the word "commander," but really are taking their own authority, and that the three scenarios have different implications?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. But of course that is very easily simplified if a letter like this is signed clearly by someone on behalf of it. Then it is clear who signed the letter and why he would have signed it in the absence of his boss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to refer you to the next document, which is at tab 10. And this is an order that comes down from the army headquarters on the 13th of August which orders changes, and basically asks to form in the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility the El Mujahedin detachment. And that it gives a code number, and that the mobilisation plan would be administered by the 3rd Corps command. Would you agree, sir, that by this order, the army headquarters was basically telling 3rd Corps to officially take under control the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is clearly what this letter indicates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look at page 2 of this document, at paragraph 1 where it says "begin immediately, and to be finished no later than 31 August." So this would mean that the commander is given some time to make this happen.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to you the next document at tab 11, which is a document dated 28 of August 1993, which is an order -- now, this is an order by the 3rd Corps command, and the order is addressed to the operations group Bosanska Krajina and the 306 Mountain Brigade. If I refer you to the second page of this document, it talks about moving the independent detachment El Mujahid to the 306 brigade. And that the junior commander of the El Mujahid would be responsible to the commander of the 306 brigade. Now, I refer you, sir, to where we have a signature and where it says that this order was not carried out. And you can also look at the original document where we have a signature as well as the word "not carried out." Would you agree with me, sir, that this is an indication that as of 28 August, close to the deadline which was given to 3rd Corps headquarters to solve the problem, that this order was not carried out and that they were still working on the problem?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the -- it's a pity that there's no indication of why it was not carried out. But that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in light of the documents I have just shown you which, of course, you did not have and you never saw before, would you agree that General Hadzihasanovic was indeed trying to solve the problem all the way back to the month of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And of course, I found these documents extremely interesting, and they would tie in exactly with my impression that there was deep suspicion of the Mujahedin and attempt to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these documents would also confirm that General Hadzihasanovic did not like the Mujahedin and that, in fact, he was against them; and also, that he believed that using force to take them under control would not be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my colleague also referred you to a conversation during examination-in-chief with a gentleman called Fazlic. And I refer you to tab 17 within your list of documents. There are three things, sir, I would like to cover with you concerning Mr. Fazlic. I would like first to refer you to the page 0131064, which is the third page of this document, at paragraph 4 where this is a meeting that you had with Mr. Fazlic. And the first thing I'd like to confirm with you is that initially, this meeting was to talk about civilian police matters, and that Mr. Fazlic basically expressed all the successes he had in terms of getting rid of the military gangs, and that he had a 62 per cent successful detection rate and only one murder unsolved at that specific time. If I refer you not to the next paragraph, but to the following paragraph where it is mentioned the subject of intimidation of Croat minorities. There was one specific issue mentioned, and that was the case of the Botic husband and wife in Travnik. I take it that from this document, you initially considered or were quite skeptic about this claim, but now you had a lot of indications that this was well -- this may well be true, that it was a classic suicide. Would that be a proper statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. I cannot remember now what those indications were, but that is certainly the situation as I understood it at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just following this paragraph where we talk about the president of the Zenica HDZ, using these deaths as an opportunity to cues the BiH of murder and to accuse them of trying to carry out ethnic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cleansing by persuading the Croats to leave Travnik. Would you agree that based on your conversation with Mr. Fazlic and your understanding of the situation at the time, he immediately took action when he heard about this situation in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was certainly what he promised to do. I'm just trying to remember whether I had any indication of a positive follow up on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your conversation with Mr. Fazlic, sir, did that indicate to you, and maybe you were well aware at the time already, that the civil authorities were still functioning during the time you were head of the regional centre Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that actually, the war situation we were in was that of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, being the governmental forces, were actually defending the national territory as the only legitimate army against two aggressors; namely, the HVO and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could put it a slightly different way. The initial aggression was entirely from the Serbs. But then, of course, it developed into a fight between the Croats and the Bosniaks who were both defending their own territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we will move on a bit later in terms of the sharing of responsibilities. But in terms of Mr. Fazlic, would you also agree, because then he went on to speak about the Mujahedin, and the first thing that he said was that the Mujahedin, he had recently imprisoned three of them, and he said that previously, the police had allowed the Mujahedin. And now, they were arrested if they committed any crimes. Would that indicate to you, first of all, a change in policy?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I do not know, because this is several months later than the correspondence we were looking at a minute ago, what was the eventual solution as far as the Mujahedin is concerned. But certainly, it is quite clear that he stated that they would be arrested if they committed any crimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he acknowledging by the same fact that the responsibility to handle crimes committed by Mujahedin in Zenica was a civilian responsibility, at least his responsibility as a civilian police chief?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but of course that does not quite tie in with what he then said, saying that they were all under command of 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, by saying that he was under command, and I come to that because I'd like you to go to the next page where you mention at the top that you were quite impressed by Mr. Fazlic, that he was a dynamic chief of police. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he impressed me certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this created a problem for you because on one hand, you thought that Mr. Fazlic was genuine, but what he was saying was not the impression that the commander of the 3rd Corps at that time, in January of 1994, Mehmet Alagic, was saying. So you had two visions of the same problem.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I think Alagic at that time was incredibly critical of the Mujahedin. But he indicated that he did have them under control, to me, although he said he would like them out of his area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we'll move on to specific documents with Mr. Alagic. But if we compare statements made to you by General Hadzihasanovic and General Alagic, who had first-hand involvement with the Mujahedin, and anything that might have been told to you by the civilian police chief, would you agree with me that you would give more weight to what would be told to you by the military commanders involved?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the comments made to you by Mr. Fazlic in January 1994, and he did not indicate to you since when these people would have been under control, if they were.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he did not say -- basically this could mean that the problem was solved, but we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he did tell you that he had just put bad criminals in jail who were Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So any -- from these documents, any further guess would be pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, another incident happened. And this will be the last one we cover before the break, was that a kidnapping in mid-October where four or five Croats were kidnapped in Travnik. Do you recall this event?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in response to a question by my colleague, you mentioned that you were not involved in this type of activity, at least initially.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not initially, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to tab number 12 in this document. Tab number 12, and I refer you to paragraph 5 on the first page, where it says "the HVO have been holding a wounded Mujahedin soldier in Busovaca jail. And as a response, the Mujahedin in Travnik have taken five new civilian hostages, and one has since been released." I now refer you to paragraph 7 where we have a conversation where it is said that "after asking Mr. Beba, who was the chief of security in Travnik, we were asking for his advice concerning the release of the Croatian hostages, and his answer was that he could do nothing for the moment. And he spoke strongly off the record about the lack of control which the Mujahedin are displaying, and he gave the following points." The first one that whatever the Mujahedin were doing, they were really going in terms of giving ammunition to the Croat propaganda. Secondly, that the commander, Alagic, of the operations group, because now we are back in October, he had other concerns, but that he will demand control when the conditions were right. And he also indicated at paragraph (c) that if the Mujahedin do not accept to work under the control of the army, that this could lead to an armed conflict. Would this information, sir, fit well in terms of all the documents we've seen earlier and the situation in January, where we are now in October, at the end of October, and we do not have the Mujahedin under control, but it is strongly acknowledged that there is a problem?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that ties in with my understanding. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to refer you now to tab 13, where we are talking specifically about General Alagic. And to the second page of this document in the middle, where we have "V1 meeting with ICRC concerning the allegations that Mujahedin are taking Croatian hostages." And I refer you there to the middle of this paragraph where it says "commander Alagic, who will attempt to pressure the Mujahedin to release the hostages. Alagic claims his efforts in the past resulted in the release of one hostage but four still remain, and he hastened to add that the Mujahedin are not under his control." If we come back to the first page, this is a document dated 29 of October 1993, and would you agree that this is a report that was prepared by team V1 attached to the coordinating centre at Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree that when Alagic is saying, or at least is portrayed as saying, that he will attempt to pressure, that a commander who had control would say "I will do something" and a commander who does not have control will say "I will attempt to do something"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this ties in exactly with my understanding that the Mujahedin were a law unto themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you now to tab number 15. And we have three documents in this tab. The first document is dated 26 of November. And this is a document which was prepared by the liaison officer of Travnik and addressed to the commander officer of the British Battalion who was at the time Lieutenant Colonel Williams. At paragraph 2 of this letter, it is said that "the operation group in Travnik has no power over the Mujahedin, and that there seemed to have been considerable efforts by all commanders to avoid blame." Also says that "Beba Salko, the gentleman that we referred to earlier, had a major falling out with Alagic over this issue." And the comment is "I think that everyone is not only embarrassed over the situation but also face is being lost because the Mujahedin are not under control." Would you agree that this also portrays the situation as you understood it at the time, in November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 3 of this letter, we mention that the two hostages which have been released are in protective custody. And the gentleman, Captain Guinness went to see these people and they seemed content to be there. And at para 4 of this document, it appears that the two that are still being detained, according to them, they say that only Alagic would be the man who has any authority over the Mujahedin. Now, if we link this paragraph with what Beba Salko was saying earlier on in the other letter, that it would need to be higher than Alagic to do something about this issue, would that once again illustrate the situation as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is of interest that they say that Alagic is the only man who had authority. That was their opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I refer you to the next page under this document, which is a letter written by Colonel Williams addressed to Brigadier Ramsey, chief of staff of BH command of UNPROFOR. And I refer you to -- this letter is written on the 5th of December. And the last three lines of the first paragraph where it says: "The release of the two missing hostages may be beyond even the power of Mehmet Alagic, commander of the 3rd Corps Bosnian Army, as it is unclear whether he even controls the Mujahedin units." Would you agree that this was the understanding of Colonel Williams, that the Mujahedin were not under control?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I refer you to the next document under this heading, which is a milinfosum dated 1 December which is referred to by Colonel Williams in his letter, and I refer you to paragraph 6 where it says: "When asked" - in the middle of the paragraph we're talking about Beba Salko - and it talks "when asked about the two hostages held by the Mujahedin in Mijovici it was stated that it would have to go higher than Alagic for their release, and that this possibly reflects that Alagic does not have absolute control contrary to what we've seen earlier, and that the Mujahedin were either an independent unit or under Opcon at army level." Would that indicate to you, sir, that this milinfosum is saying either one of two things, the Mujahedin is still a unit which has not been integrated, or, again, that it is an army asset and it has nothing to do with the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the de jure situation on the ground was at that time, as far as the Mujahedin is concerned. But clearly, the opinion expressed here is that Alagic would not be able to effect the release of these hostages, and it would have to go higher than him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. We will stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to adjourn for the break. And we will resume at 10 or 15 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when we departed just prior to the break, I was asking you whether you could confirm that the information we went through this morning fell in line with your views concerning the Mujahedin. And you basically mentioned that whether or regardless of the de jure situation of the Mujahedin, for sure the de facto situation was that they did not exercise control over the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to refer you, sir, to tab number 18 in the series of documents that I've shown you. And tab number 18, and I draw your attention to the last paragraph of this document at paragraph 6, page 3, where it is mentioned that V1 met with Commander Alagic who informed that he was -- he would shortly become the commander of 3 Corps, but that he would attempt to assist with the problems of hostage-taking by Mujahedin. I would also like to refer you to tab 16 before asking my question, tab 16 being your own letter addressed to Mrs. Popovic, in which you say on the 1st of January, and I refer to the middle paragraph, where you say that you had two meetings with General Alagic to discuss the matter of her husband, and that General Alagic had assured me that he was doing all he could to find out what has happened and that he would let you know. Can you confirm on the basis of these two documents that even though the Mujahedin were not de facto under control, that General Alagic did tell you and was sincere in saying that he would do everything he could to find out what was going on and to solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he assured me of this on more than one occasion. And I was confident that he meant what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, given, sir, that this situation we are talking about, your letter dated 1 January, and the first document, which is a report from Team V1 from the coordination centre Travnik, dates back in November, would you agree that if the situation with regards to the Mujahedin was unclear in November, December of 1993 and January of 1994, that it was even less so or less clear in October when General Hadzihasanovic was commanding the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was clear that although this had been going -- this problem had been going for several months, no progress had been made at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to move to another topic, which is the issue of Vares which you covered in your examination-in-chief. Now, I don't want to cover the event itself given that General Hadzihasanovic is not charged with any events. But I'd like to refer you to tab number 2 and to discuss with you the strategic importance of Vares. And my question, of course, would be that do you agree that Vares was indeed of strategic importance to the 3rd Corps and to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was extremely important because it was a Croat-HVO enclave. And once Vares was in ABiH hands, then the ABiH Army could move from the north 2 Corps, 3 Corps, 6 Corps, 4 Corps, all the way down to Gornji Vakuf without passing through any Bosniak areas. Because they could skirt Vitez and Busovaca over the mountains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to refer you to the second document. This is a report that was drafted before you ever arrived in Bosnia on the 2nd of June. But I'd like you -- to refer you to paragraph number 5 where it says that "the Bosnian Serb Army actions suggest that there may be an effort underway to take Maglaj and to cut off the Maglaj finger to form yet another Muslim pocket." At paragraph (b), we say that the Doboj/Serb salient may be pushed east to connect with the Bosnian Serb to the east, and that if this were to occur, two things would result, which is the creation of yet another pocket, which is the Tuzla pocket; and a much more useful corridor between east and west for Serbian areas, and one more acceptable to the Croats. And that the effects of this, at paragraph 6, would be a flood of refugees similar to what happened when Jajce fell. And that Zenica would be overwhelmed with refugees, which would destabilise and weaken the BiH position in Zenica and reinforce the Croatian population of the Travnik-Kiseljak line. Can you relate to the operational situation as described here on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the Maglaj finger did become a Maglaj pocket, but they did not succeed in the -- the BSA did not succeed in the second task, which was linking up Doboj with the east and thus creating a Tuzla pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can acknowledge the fact that the ABiH did lose and that the Maglaj finger in fact became a pocket?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this, of course, was a very dangerous sign for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that in this respect, the operation in Vares later that year was as in some sort not only to create the route up to the north, but also to prevent the salient operation joining the Serb east and the west?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to refer you now to tab number 4 of this document. Sir, tab number 4 is a report which is dated 21 August 1993. It is a report which was addressed by General Hadzihasanovic which you can see from page 27, and it is a situation report which covers the situation in which the 3rd Corps was on 21 August 1993. I take it that such a document would have been very useful to you in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been extremely useful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document, if we -- if I take you to page 5 in the middle, there is a comment in the paragraph called "conclusion" where it says, and -- about the middle where it is mentioned "we think that we should pay full attention to this while engaging our forces and direct our actions towards preventing the introduction of the aggressors' forces into the said areas so as to avoid the repetition of the Zepce case." I know this is just a small part of a big document. But would you agree that General Hadzihasanovic by this paragraph is assessing in terms of operational planning the way the forces must be employed in order to avoid losing any further territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and more specifically, in this case, the situation such as Zepce?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would certainly be my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that this kind of report which assesses and -- the situation in terms of a full evaluation of the enemy forces, a full evaluation of friendly forces or our own forces, a full evaluation of problems and challenges is the kind of assessment that would be made by a reasonable commander, and that such a document would not contain any misinformation as a commander always wants his superior headquarters to be fully informed of the situation he is in?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that a report such as this written by any military commander would have to be as truthful as he understood it. Otherwise, it would be worthless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you, sir, now to tab number 18 of the document simply to move to page 2 of this document where we are talking about -- it is a conversation that you had with a gentleman called Zubaca who was the commander of the operation leading to the takeover of Vares by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I simply refer you to the top paragraph where it says: "BiH authorities are encouraging Croats to remain in Vares, inviting refugees to return, and that they will not seek revenge." Do you recall either a conversation or the contents of such a conversation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I just read that a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may direct you a little further down, sir, to the paragraph that begins with a question where it says "what is the future for Croats in Vares." And the answer was: "They are welcome to stay because historically, Muslims and Croats have always gotten along well in Vares, and the BiH wanted a political solution, but this was not possible with the HVO." Does that also reflect the position of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly what Zubaca said at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And lastly, sir, if we move to -- three paragraphs down where the question was "now the BiH has a secure route to Tuzla." And the answer to this question was: "Yes, BiH 4, 6, 2 and 3 Corps are now connected, and Vares is the crucial link. The new road to the north is no longer so important." Would that indicate to you that Vares was a multicorps operation which would require a lot of planning, and that is taken at least at the operational level if not the strategic level?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because it involved both 2 and 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may now refer you to a new document which I would like to give you, it is a document dated 4 November 1993 which is a report from the regional centre Zenica. And I bring your attention to page 3 of this document where it says: "HRC's assessment for November 1993." Would you recognise this as being your own assessment, the type of which you would do on a weekly basis, to report on what was the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is certainly my input into this report. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may refer you to the next page, the third paragraph, which reads as follows: "It is certainly clear that the capture of Vares has given the BiH a significant strategic advantage, and for a start they are now able to link up 4, 6, 3 and 2 BiH Corps, thus enabling them to have a front running from Mostar in the south to Tuzla and beyond in the north." Was this your assessment of the situation with regards to the Vares operation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question would deal more specifically with the Vares operation. Is that the type of planning and the type of operations and the type of work on a daily basis which is the work of a corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A corps commander would certainly be assessing strategic priorities and making recommendations to his superiors about what is to be done next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suggest to you, sir, that it has been said that a corps commander working at the operational level would normally think at least four days ahead. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, at least four days ahead, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I move on to a different issue, that of discipline, would you agree with me, sir, that the issue of discipline is of paramount importance to any army, and that it is what makes an army successful or an army that will be defeated?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Agreed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that when we talk about discipline, it means that a commander must be sensible to the fact that army regulations will be respected. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that, for example, in times of war, a violation which would be minor in peacetime can have major consequences in war. And I give you an example: Leaving one's duty station in peacetime may have little consequences but in wartime may have absolute disastrous consequences?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that discipline would also be to enforce national law or common-law crimes and to take action if soldiers commit common-law crimes?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also to abide by international law and to take action against -- if soldiers commit any events against international law?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the object of discipline, of course, is to make one's force operational and effective. But would you agree with me that what a commander has to do is has to try to prevent violations, to stop them, and to take measures to ensure that if there are violations they will be taken care of?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sometimes, depending on the level of the commander, sometimes he will take action himself, and sometimes he will take action by referring a matter to, for example, legal authorities?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that once a specific matter has been taken care of, either by the commander himself or by a commander at a subordinate level, or by a legal institution, whatever it may be, that in such a case, the commander has respected what his responsibilities are?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I'm not quite sure -- I mean, if he is asked advice from legal authorities and he gets that advice, then presumably he would act on it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of course, it is important for the commander to realise what his duties are, and if there are, like in this case, civilian authorities which are still operating, then it's important to understand what was the role of the commander with respect to the law and what was the role of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we have -- we went through two examples. The first one is when we talked about the work of Mr. Fazlic as the civilian police chief. He would take care of the civilian common-law crimes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your examination-in-chief, we covered a situation of a priest named Stipan Radic. And you thought that this gentleman was a good man in a tough situation, that he reported some issues concerning the army.
