And your answer to that question was, I quote here to page 18 of the transcript on page 67, "I think they did turn out to be true because when they were followed up by Bosniak commanders, they accepted there was a problem. And in invariably, there was an improvement in the situation." Can you confirm, sir, these were your views at the time and your understanding of the situation that when Mr. Radic did bring some problems to the attention of the authorities, whether civilian or military, actions were taken to try and improve the situation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to the issue of the military situation on the ground. And I'm a bit running out of time already, so I have to go a bit quicker. But I'd like to confirm with you, you've mentioned already the situation of the HVO and the Serbs. But I'd like to suggest to you a few issues which might have an impact on the exercise of command by the commanding general of a corps. And, for example, the fact that the commander had to deal with a Serb front line of more than 300 kilometres, would that be a factor that would weigh heavily on a commander's planning?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the issue of roads and where roads were not accessible or blocked, either to Sarajevo or up north to Tuzla, that this was also something that the commander must have been concerned about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that the issue of refugees was a big problem; in fact, you mentioned in your examination-in-chief that there were more than 50.000 refugees in Zenica alone?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would this be a problem that would definitely impact on the work of the commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been inevitably a big concern, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the embargo on weapons that we mentioned, would that also be something that would affect the planning because the commander must always plan ahead in terms of: I have less weapons so how can I distribute my forces to face stronger weapons from the other side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fact of having a new army, which is something that you felt you were uneasy about, having both a new army that was less then one year old, is that something that may create a more difficult situation for a commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. I would have thought that both sides, although they had some senior officers who had served in the JNA, inevitably, some of the more junior officers were recently recruited, and their calibre was unknown, and therefore some of them I am sure were not fully reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I may direct you now to tab number 4 of the document which is again this report I was referring to, and to page 22. Page 22 is the number of killed and wounded from the beginning of the war until 31 July 1993. And if we look at page number 23, the total, it refers to 1.570 persons or soldiers killed, and 6.478 soldiers wounded. Would that be a factor that would weigh heavily on the planning of the commander and where he would put his priorities?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Any high-casualty rate or any casualty rate would inevitably be a major factor in planning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may refer you to a little earlier in the same report, and I'm talking here at page 14, the second paragraph where it says that the corps command itself was at a 66 per cent establishment rate. Would that be a factor that would make the life of a commander much more difficult?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, inevitably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we move down to -- down at the page, the total number for the corps itself, which was at 73.34 per cent, would also -- would that also make the situation more difficult for the commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to manpower, in response to a question by my colleague in examination-in-chief, you said that there was much more people or much more people of military age on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, however, that even though you have much more people, that one, if you don't have weapons for those people, they cannot be very useful; and that unless and until these people are trained, it takes a lot and imposes a burden on the commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The Serb strength was in their weaponry; the Bosniak strength was in their manpower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the situation in Central Bosnia or were you aware of the fact that the Serbs and the HVO were linking up together in terms of fighting the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly indications that in certain places, this was happening, yes. For example, when the Croats move north out of Vares, it is clear that they moved into Serb-occupied Bosnia, and then down to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Were you also aware that at some instances, whereas the line facing the Serb was previously occupied as a joint venture with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, that the HVO withdrew from the line, thus causing a big problem of manpower for the commander of the corps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot think of a specific incidence where this happened, but undoubtedly it did once the two armies split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, also in the same document at tab 4, I'd like to refer you to page 10. Now, I wish I'd had time to go through some more of these issues in detail, but if we look just at the first paragraph under "command and control problems," commander Hadzihasanovic here is highlighting the fact of three very important factors with which he is having problems, which is the competence of personnel, communications, and motivation. Would these be factors that would make his life and the exercise of command more difficult?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are three key factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't have time to refer you to these specific, but the fact that he brings these issues to the higher headquarters, would that also be an indication that he is considering these problems as being serious?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And of course, the point about the competence of personnel ties in with my comment which I gave a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, would you agree that the presence of internationals in Central Bosnia also could make the exercise of command more difficult, whereas on the average General Hadzihasanovic could be visited by ten different persons each day who all wanted to see the corps commander, and that he had to answer to all these requests?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you also aware about the fact that Zenica, where the corps headquarters was located, was being shelled on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, during your conversation, and this is at tab 14, but I will move through, one issue was highlighted by General Hadzihasanovic which was the fact that two helicopters had been hijacked by the HVO and for a very long period of time were not available for casualty evacuations. Would that also be a significant factor in the planning and the priorities established by the commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was certainly a big blow to the ABiH Army, and it's one that we ourselves pursued over many months to try and get them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, one of the issues that was highlighted by General Hadzihasanovic was the fact that when the opposing force commits crimes, that it also makes it very difficult for a commanding general to control his troops because they feel and they would like to seek revenge.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, all of these factors, sir, you will agree with me they don't change the fact that the commander is responsible?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nevertheless, when he establishes his priorities and when he decides what he is going to do and when, all of these factors have a very important bearing?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are factors which he would have to weigh up very carefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go on by looking at the exercise of command. And if I tell you, for example, that General Hadzihasanovic, because he thought that he had 300 kilometres of front line, himself at his own initiative forced a meeting of all corps generals and proposed the creation of an additional corps; basically, that his corps area would be split into two. Would that be a sign of a responsible general?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a general who is given an organisation where he has 19 brigades to lead and who, by himself, initiates the creation of operational groups, kind of, something like divisions, in order to facilitate his control over his troops, would that be a sign of a commander who is trying to do his best to control his people?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would certainly be a sensible course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I suggest to you that General Hadzihasanovic introduced a system of identification cards to ensure that we would know at all times who was in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would that also be a good measure to control the people?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not aware that that had happened, but it would certainly be a sensible move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I propose to you that General Hadzihasanovic introduced a system of vehicle registration to ensure that vehicles used by the army could be identified as such, would also -- would that also be a very good measure to control the forces under his command?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I suggest to you that General Hadzihasanovic issued multiple orders that you probably have never seen because you did not have access to the orders, telling his commanders at all levels to abide by the law, would that also be the sign of a reasonable commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a quite correct exercise of authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the same General Hadzihasanovic took a number of measures to ensure that commanders subordinate to him would take measures to prevent and to stop violations of discipline and of any criminal act, and that he issued orders to that effect, would that also be a sign of a responsible commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General Hadzihasanovic, if I propose to you, ensured that the military justice system was works by authorising his commanders to do special military courts, and even giving them the power of death over his troops, their troops, would that be a commander who cares about discipline and the enforcement of law?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if General Hadzihasanovic thought that the justice system was not working well enough in order that this created problems for him from an operational point of view and that he then complained to his higher headquarters "do something about the justice system because it is giving me problems on the ground," would that also be the sign of a reasonable commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that makes absolute sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if a general succeeded, despite all the conditions that we have covered since the beginning of my cross-examination, if such a general had succeeded in fulfilling his mission in that he took a corps which was nonexistent, he built that corps, and if we only look at the difference between June when you were there and November when you were there, the success and the improvement in the workings and the discipline of this corps, would that be a sign of a very good and effective commander?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if in such a situation, the commander took the measures even to train his people and to create a training centre, despite wartime conditions, to ensure that his troops would be trained, would that also be a commander who cares not only about discipline, but about accomplishing his mission?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in view of what we discussed previously, that would be most important and a correct course, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the one issue that -- I saw a document yesterday in which you yourself sent a document - and I don't have this document with me, but I'm sure you will recall - you sent that document within the United Kingdom chain of command. And you were saying in this document "that doesn't apply to me, I'm a retired general. But there's a lot of military officers here who come in this theatre of operations expecting that if they do good they will either be promoted or get special rewards." And that you were highlighting this issue to your chain of command or your ex-chain of command to ensure and say: Come on, guys, we have guys operating on the ground here and they should be rewarded and they should get reports if they do a good job. Do you recall writing this message?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly recall writing along those lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I tell you, General, that General Hadzihasanovic in his report that we saw was asking for better pay for his soldiers and for better conditions for his soldiers and better rewards for his soldiers, despite wartime conditions, is that a commander that is caring about his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's certainly a facet of command which is very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we saw a bit earlier that it appears that one of the options General Hadzihasanovic had with respect to the Mujahedin was to use force. And it would appear on the documents that he decided not to. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you agree, sir, that if we were to challenge this decision today, that any one who wanted to challenge this, it would be necessary to have information with respect to what resources he had?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the fact that: Who were the Mujahedin in terms of how many there were, where they were, what weapons they had, what resources they had, and what techniques they used, that this would have been important before using force against any enemy force?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were potentially dangerous, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that it would also be important to have a full appraisal of the operational situation in terms of knowing exactly if he takes a company off the line to address this problem, or if a company is enough, what are the consequences and will that lead to the line being broken and him losing territory? Anyone challenging his decision today would have to have such information?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one would have to have a very clear indication of who one was up against, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you also agree that it would be necessary to challenge such a decision to understand that whether General Hadzihasanovic had the authorisation from his supreme headquarters before opening up a third front?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, it appears as though his superior headquarters was recommending this line, but clearly if he decided to follow that, he would need to go back to them in view of what he'd replied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've met General Hadzihasanovic. I'd like you to turn to tab number 3 of this document. Tab number 3 is document dated 7 October. And this was at a time when you were not yet head of the regional centre, but you were designate head of mission. And at that time, you met with General Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Merdan, and this is a three-page report dealing with all kinds of issues with General Hadzihasanovic. Do you recall this moment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I refer you to paragraph 10 where it says "Hadzihasanovic is clearly an intelligent man, soft-spoken, articulate, polite, but quite convinced in his views and opinions. And he made clear that the elements of the BiH at least have the will and the capacity to continue the fight until they achieve their goals. Also imply that money was not a problem because he was getting donations from abroad." And if we would go back to the beginning of the document, he also says that this money is not coming only from the Islamic sources, that if he is reflecting the views of Izetbegovic, that peace might be a long way off. Now, this assessment of General Hadzihasanovic, would you concur that this is the assessment that you agree that he was yet tough but totally professional, that he was absolutely clear and straight in his dealings with you? This is something that you mention in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are my views at the time, and I've no reason in the intervening years to change them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mention that he was clear -- it was clear that he had authority and that he was -- so would I take that this would mean that he was in command of the corps and that he was doing his best to make the corps work?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly my view. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mention something that you were of the impression that he was being well aware of what was going on in his area. Would that mean, sir, that being well aware of what is going on means that he knows what type of war he's in, what type of scenario he's facing, and he knows what his next move will be?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that doesn't necessarily mean being aware of a specific incident which might happen?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go on, you say that you were -- he was absolutely clear and straight in his dealings with -- sorry, that the fact that he was giving straight answers and -- straight answers would -- that could be understood as being that you knew that he -- when he gave you an answer, he was not giving you false information and that you knew you could get the right story from him?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly believed what he told me, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your examination-in-chief that although you were not checking on him, when things developed later on, they always proved that what he had told you was actually what he was really telling you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I look at General Hadzihasanovic the way you met this man on the ground in 1993, and when I look at -- I propose to you that everything I said in terms of the measures taken, not only in terms of discipline but the measures to train, the measures to communicate, the measures to inform his higher headquarters, the measures to inform the international representatives dealing with him, I would like to ask you one question of opinion with respect to the character of General Hadzihasanovic: Would you think in your assessment of what we have covered today and what you saw from the man in 1993 that he would be the type of commander who would not take action to discipline someone if he had the occasion to do so?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly considered him to be a good general, which would certainly imply what you've said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I'd like to take this opportunity to highlight the fact I saw from the documents that tomorrow is your 69th birthday, and I wish to wish you a happy birthday. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That ends the cross-examination on behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn now to the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Dixon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only a few questions on behalf of Mr. Kubura. You said in your examination-in-chief that you travelled to the town of Vares on the 4th of November 1993 with Mr. William Stutt. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's correct that when you arrived there, you found that the Bosnian Army was in control of the town of Vares, the HVO having withdrawn without putting up any fight. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you noticed damage in the town, broken windows and broken doors you mentioned. But that you were not in a position to say whether that damage was caused by the Bosnian Army that was there or by the HVO forces that had withdrawn. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified to the fact that you recognised the 7th Brigade when you were approaching Vares. There were troops from the 7th Brigade, you said, on the outskirts of Vares. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you probably identified them because they were wearing insignia on their shoulders which were specific to the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot remember quite how we identified them, but we certainly did identify them as 7 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And may it have been because of the insignia that they were wearing --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's most likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went into the town of Vares, however, you said that you were not able to identify the units of the Bosnian Army that were in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw a number of soldiers in the town but you weren't able to specify which units the soldiers were from in any detail?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was an awful lot of shooting going on so it was not possible to stop and identify them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware of the fact, as this was a multicorps operations, that there were a number of units from a number of corps involved in the operation to take control of Vares?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers that you then saw in the centre of the town, would it be fair to say that they were from many of those units that had been involved in the operation to take control of Vares?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to say from which units they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it is possible that they were from the different units that had been involved in the operation to take control of Vares?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is certainly possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Sir Martin. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has just a few questions for the witness. Re-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, we've never actually met. My name is Daryl Mundis. I'm one of the Prosecutors on the case. Mr. Withopf whom you met earlier is in the process of packing his office. Today is in fact his last day here at the Tribunal. I have, sir, just a few questions for you. In response to questions from the Defence for Mr. Hadzihasanovic, you indicated that it was your opinion that the 3rd Corps did not have de facto control over the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just ask the usher, I'm sorry, to perhaps move the ELMO. I'm having a bit of difficulty seeing the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on how many occasions did you actually observe any Mujahedin or foreign fighters in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw very few in Zenica itself. And occasionally, one spotted individuals when one was driving around -- particularly around the mountains, which I did not often do, the mountain road to Novi Travnik. So they were not very much in evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how much information, if any, did you have about possible military operations in which 3rd Corps units and Mujahedin units were operating together?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little. That is why I was constantly asking about the Mujahedin. We knew very little about them and their activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would it in any way surprise you if there were other individuals who testified that Mujahedin were spearheading operations for 3rd Corps units?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd be very interested. But I cannot think of any specific examples, although Vares, of course, could certainly be one as they were on the outskirts of Vares. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as a former commander of the Royal Marines, can you tell us a little bit about the need for command and control with respect to the first marine or the first unit, for example, to hit the beach and to spearhead the operation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command and control, of course, is absolutely fundamental. And the more complicated an operation, the more important it is. Command and control and, of course, communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And specifically, sir, with respect to the first soldier or soldiers or a rekkie unit that's sent into a village, how important would that be for a commander to have a degree of control over those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crucially important because he would be waiting for the information to come back as to how the operation was going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn briefly to another issue, that being discipline. Can you tell us a little bit about the relationship between discipline and the importance of a commander's role in preventing crimes from happening and/or punishing crimes which he becomes aware of that have happened, the relationship between those and discipline.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think both are entirely interrelated. A commander must be confident that his officers and men are behaving correctly and not doing anything which they are not allowed to do. And therefore, if he discovers that they are, then it's clearly essential that he exercises discipline effectively as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it from that answer, sir, that maintaining good order and discipline would be a very important component of a senior military commander's responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fundamentally important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, we, at least based on my own experience in the military, we refer to good order and discipline by the initials GOD. Have you known of that term?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an interesting -- I like it, but I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my colleagues from the Defence put to you about ten different scenarios or ten different factors would be a better way of characterising it, ten different factors that impacted upon the situation facing General Hadzihasanovic, including the length of the front line, difficulties with refugees, difficulties with roads being blocked, et cetera. And clearly, based on your answers, he was in a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What impact, if any, did those factors have on his responsibilities and duties to prevent crimes from happening or to punish perpetrators for crimes that he became aware of?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, it was a very hectic period for him. But that would in no way stop him exercising full command over disciplinary matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were shown today a series of documents and a transcript of a phone intercept or a phone conversation. I take it from your responses that the information contained in that series of documents was new to you today.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I only wish I'd had it all ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it from that answer, sir, that at no point did General Hadzihasanovic in any discussion tell you about steps he might have been taking with respect to higher commands concerning the information in these documents?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you also were shown a document that did not have a signature on it, that had the signature block of General Hadzihasanovic but no signature. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of course, based again on your experience, can you tell us about any type of situations where military units are using means of communication that would not have a signature on it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar at all with -- unless nowadays emails, of course, don't have signatures. But otherwise, a normal letter would certainly have a signature on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there would be other types of military documents that would not have signatures, electronically transmitted documents?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, the documents that ECMM sent, the reports that you sent, those reports don't bear signatures?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, based on military needs or military communication systems, there would be, then, certain types of systems where there are no signatures?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Sir Martin, you've answered all of our questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir Martin, I will have a few questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you something about the subject of control. On a number of occasions in answering questions, you referred to the question of Mujahedin and as to whether they were under control or out of control. As a military man and a very high-ranking officer, could you define "control" when one has a command over a particular geographic area. How would you define that control.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the elements of the forces in your area were doing -- carrying out your orders and that you knew exactly what they were doing and they were not doing anything which was unacceptable to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in military terms, control over a certain geographic area where a state of war has been declared, is that control implemented over civilian, military, paramilitary elements? How far can that control go in your opinion? And over whom is that control exercised?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in a war situation, inevitably, the rules change somewhat and military commanders can, within their powers, which will be given to them, direct what civilians do, within certain parameters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has produced a document on the mission you had under the European Union. It is DH88 and it envisages three tasks or roles. The quest for a long-term peaceful solution, respect of human rights, and the rule of law. Would you subscribe to that mission which had three axes, the political, the rights of human rights, and the rule of law? Was indeed the mission that was entrusted to you on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, except that -- I mean, those were fundamental principles under which we were operating. But at our level, I suppose we were considering taking more into account practical steps that we needed to take on the ground. But those certainly were the overriding principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in practice, you had an individual to deal with involved with the kidnapping of Mr. Popovic. Because among the documents produced by the Defence, we have the letter that you sent to Mrs. Popovic in which you say that General Alagic has given you assurances that he would do everything necessary. In your opinion, the kidnapping of a civilian, does that fall within the frameworks of your mission; that is, to ensure respect of human rights?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would certainly come under our responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the extent that you were aware that somebody was kidnapped by an unknown or known group of people and you were informed by the victim, were you concerned about the destiny of that gentleman, Mr. Popovic, as you were informed about it? And by saying that General Alagic will take care of it, does that morally relieve you of your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour. But it is one that I kept pressing to get an answer right until the time I left Zenica to move back town to Mostar in April. But, sadly, I never got an answer, and only found out what had happened to Popovic subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you left to go to Mostar, and seeing that no progress had been made, an army has a hierarchy and above General Alagic there must have been another authority. Wasn't it then your duty to take it to a higher level, to the political level? Because it appears that you were told that this person was under the control of an element that was out of control. Wouldn't it then be necessary to take steps in favour of the family whose member had been kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But of course, the situation in Central Bosnia, there was no Bosniak political authority that had the same authority as the military authority, if -- I hope I've made myself clear. As far as the key people in Central Bosnia on the Bosniak side were the Bosniak commanders. And if they could not achieve what I asked them to achieve, referring it to the political side in Central Bosnia, to the president of the Zenica SDA, for example, would have not achieved anything, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it appears that you're telling us that the competent authority was not the political authority, but rather, the local commander who had full powers. Is that the gist of your answer?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. As I mentioned before, in Bosnia the military and the political were inextricably intertwined. But in Central Bosnia, it was clear that it was the military commanders who on the Bosniak side who were really in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you when you realised that General Alagic was doing what he could but that clearly it was not up to his level, why didn't you feel it necessary to raise this issue either with the 3rd Corps command or Ambassador Thebault when he arrived; that is, to take it up with the supreme command?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, Ambassador Thebault had gone by this time because I was the head of the regional centre. And I felt that if the commander of 3 Corps, I rested my hopes in the commander of 3 Corps achieving the release of Popovic. There was no one really else who had the power to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you left to go to Mostar, who was the 3rd Corps commander as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I left for Mostar, the commander of 3 Corps had passed to General Mahmuljin whose name came up earlier on in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you didn't have any form of contact with General Mahmuljin, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him before I left. But when I left to return to Mostar, it was to join the EU administration of Mostar. And therefore, I was cut off completely from the EC monitor mission. Therefore, I had to leave any follow-up action for outstanding matters to my successor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. The Judges have no more questions for the witness. But does Defence counsel have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have a few brief questions I would like to ask. Further cross-examined by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked by the Presiding Judge concerning the jurisdiction or the power of the military commander. And I would like to simply suggest to you that if a commander is in a zone of occupation, that in such a case, we all know, and military officers know, that when you are into a zone of occupation, then the commander is responsible not only for the military but for the civilian aspects. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, if we look in Iraq today, some people have said, although this is disputed, that the United States of America are, in fact, occupying Iraq. Would that be your views?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly a view that is stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if so, the military commander, his jurisdiction goes way beyond the military force and applies to the maintenance of civil order.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we're talking about Bosnia, presumably we're talking about Bosnia now, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- no, sorry, we're talking about Iraq. If Iraq was a situation of military occupation as some people say it is, then the authority of the military commander goes way beyond the military force.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if that is the situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've acknowledged that in a situation such as Bosnia, the civil authority was still functioning, that civilian police was still working.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also acknowledge that the civil emergency was still operating?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil emergency?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Civil emergency. Civil protection, sorry. I was looking for the English word.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Civil protection was also operating.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there were elements of the civilian infrastructure which were functioning, yes, to a greater or lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was still a legitimate government in force?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And given that you also understand that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was fighting on its own territory, would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were not into a situation of occupation.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in such a scenario, if a commander is not into a situation of occupation, what determines his powers will be the law?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look at the law, we will know whether or not he had any powers beyond the military force?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I move on to your -- the situation of having your own role as part of ECMM. Now, of course, the name of your mission was European Community Monitoring Mission. Can we take from the name that the overall objective beyond promoting and focussing modes of action, that the main focus was to monitor the situation and to report it back to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Monitoring and reporting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not there to investigate or to police the area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or to solve problems?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where we could, we did. Particularly on the humanitarian front. But we were not -- we did not have authority to go out and arrest people or do anything like that. We could only use our own pressures to try and achieve results, particularly in the humanitarian field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, cases such as the Popovic case, now this case is now made very -- seems to be a special case, but there were numerous incidents which were reported to you through all of your teams were different violations committed by different people were reported to you at all times, almost on a daily basis. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many, many incidents reported, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in some cases, you had -- it was easier for you to use your good offices or your pressure to try and bring a solution to a problem, but that was not your first role.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you did report a situation such as the Popovic, when you wrote a report which went all the way up to Zagreb, the world knew about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the politicians wanted to do something in addition to your own mandate, they could -- there's numerous things they could have done.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I could just make one point clear. When you say all politicians would have known about, for example, Popovic, we were not in a position to tell Zagreb headquarters what they were going to put in their reports which went on to capitals. So we were never aware -- we never saw the final report which went off from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But the -- once the report arrived in Zagreb, the mission itself as it was created - it is a kind of collective agreement of states - as it was created, those people were mandated to run the ECMM operations; they knew about the situation, and they could elect to report or not and to recommend actions or not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question concerning the issue of control. You responded to the question by the Presiding Judge that to you, control was you can issue orders. You know that your orders will be respected or will be enforced. And you know that those units will not do things without you knowing them. And that is control.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, without going into the technical details, would you agree with me that there are situations where a commander has an area of responsibility, and within this area there are forces which are not under his control?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I give you one example, if you are a brigade commander and you have an area of responsibility, it may be that the corps commander will locate artillery resources in your area. These resources will be in location. Chances are you will be informed because you want to know who is in your land, but you have no control over division artillery resources placed in your brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but you would certainly as a commander insist on being made aware of exactly what other forces were in your area and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those forces that are -- this is one example of forces placed in your area which you have no control over, but there are even other scenarios where you don't control forces in your specific area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But again, you would have to know what is going on. Otherwise, you could not exercise command in your own area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon has no further questions. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a couple questions following from those put by Your Honours. Further examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir Martin, you told us based on your experience the military authorities and not the political authorities were really in charge in Central Bosnia, were you making reference to the de jure situation or the de facto situation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the de facto situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the basis for you reaching that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is just, for example, on the Croat side, if I wanted really the man at the top, I would go not to the military leader but to the political leader, a man called Dario Kordic. That was just a fact. And on the Bosniak side, I would go to the commander of 3 Corps. Because one knew after having been there a very short time who was the boss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir Martin, this concludes your examination. I'd like to thank you for having come here on a number of occasions to testify as a witness for the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber would like to thank you for the contribution you have made to establishing the truth. We wish you a good trip home and we wish you all the best when you return home and in the course of your activities. We hope you have many interesting such activities. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, could you tell us what the schedule is for next week. We will commence with the hearings on Tuesday next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have provided the Chamber and the Defence with a letter indicating the specific order. We will have on Tuesday commencing at 14.15 hours Mr. Junhov, followed by the two witnesses for which the Chamber has ordered their testimony via videolink. I might also add, Mr. President that, as I indicated yesterday, the Prosecution is prepared to either read into the record or I can reduce to writing information pertaining to the Trial Chamber's oral order of 17 May 2004 and the meeting which was held between the Trial Chamber's legal officer and the senior trial attorney, Mr. Withopf. I anticipate if we were to do that on the record, it would take some 15 to 20 minutes. Again, alternatively, I can reduce that to writing and provide it to the Chamber and the Defence certainly by Tuesday morning or Tuesday midday prior to our sitting on Tuesday. I leave it up to Your Honours whether -- which course of action you would propose we take with respect to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It would be possible for you to make oral submissions. You could do this for about 15 minutes today perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. I note the time, and I think we're due for a break. I could certainly do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, it would be best to have the break now. It is a quarter to 1.00. We will resume at 10 past 1.00. And we'll have sufficient time to deal with the issue. So we will resume at 10 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I shall give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, before Mr. Mundis commences, there is a matter affecting the schedule for next week. And I don't believe we have translation on the transcript yet because I don't have it on my screen, Your Honours. So I should wait for that, I would presume. I'm informed that the transcript is working. Your Honour, it concerns -- there's probably no need to go into private session, but it concerns the order that Your Honours made this morning concerning the protective measures for a particular witness. Your Honours, in light of the very clear ruling that Your Honours have made, it is the Defence's position that the only step that we can, therefore, take in order to vary the protective measures is to apply to the Blaskic Appeals Chamber itself in order that the matter be reconsidered by the Chamber that is still seized of the matter, not the Trial Chamber any longer, but the Appeals Chamber in that case. Your Honours, clear, this is not an appeal of Your Honours' decision, but it is an application which, it is our understanding under Rule 75 we are entitled to make. Either party, either the Prosecution or the Defence with supply to vary the existing protective measures. And we do plan to take such an application immediately. We will be in a position to file that application on Tuesday morning after the break on Monday. Your Honours, it is our understanding that that will then affect the scheduling for next week as in our view the witness cannot be heard until the Blaskic Appeals Chamber has ruled on our application. Your Honours will be aware that there is a videolink planned for another witness for next week. So in our view, the videolink procedure can still go ahead. But only in respect of one witness and not the other while we await that decision to be made. It is our submission that that matter does need to be resolved before the witness testifies. As Your Honour will recall, this witness indicated to Your Honours that he would not be able to testify unless he got protective measures because of the position that he holds in his church. And it is, therefore, essential that this matter is resolved before he testifies so that he is in a position to know what exactly the measures will be that will apply to him, if any. So Your Honours, as a result of this application, there will be in our view a knock-on affect the schedule for next week will have to be altered to some extent with one of the witnesses, Your Honours will know which one, not being in a position to testify via videolink until the decision is made by the Blaskic Appeals Chamber. As a result of that decision, which hopefully can be taken within the time that the Prosecution case is still open, another date will have to be found for that witness. I understand, and this might well become clear now in the outline that Mr. Mundis is going to give, that the Prosecution case might well last most of this month and into June and most of June. So there will be an opportunity once the decision has been rendered by the Appeals Chamber for the witness to be recalled depending on what the outcome of that decision is. I'm grateful, Your Honours, for that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Simply to tell the Chamber that this will be a joint application. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the question of the witness, let us first go into private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to the videotapes, perhaps I can address those in just a few moments. Let me again state that we are not in a position to call any additional witnesses other than the one scheduled for Tuesday for next week. I leave it to the Trial Chamber with respect to the witness who is scheduled for Wednesday morning, the first witness, with respect to a videolink and I raised that simply because, Mr. President, as you're undoubtedly aware, there is a huge economic cost in providing testimony by way of videolink. And if we were only talking about one witness, that may not necessarily be the best use of the Tribunal's resources, although I obviously leave that to Your Honours' discretion. We still want that witness to testify whether it's next week or a few weeks after that pending the resolution of the matter with respect to the second witness. Let me just briefly state another possibility with respect to that second witness, however, Mr. President: One other available option would be that he be permitted to testify pursuant to the Chamber's earlier order, that is, the order rendered this morning; and in the event the Appeals Chamber then varied the order, that one remedy perhaps could be to then make that testimony available to the public. That would be another issue that, again, I leave to Your Honours for their consideration. With respect to the timing issues and the medical condition, another suggestion would be for the Prosecution to adduce his evidence by way of Rule 89 (D), having him simply affirm his statement and then make him available for cross-examination, albeit on a shortened time frame, perhaps over the course of three days sitting 30 minutes per day. Again, I leave those issues to the Chamber. The Prosecution, of course, still would like those witnesses to testify prior to the closing of our case. And if, in fact, an additional delay results due to that, we would seek leave to call those witnesses at a later time. But again, because of the Chamber's prior order, it's completely in the Chamber's hands with respect to the timing of those two witnesses whose testimony is to be heard via videolink. If I could, Mr. President, turn, and Your Honours, turn to the other issue that I wanted to address you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. I shall give you the floor in a minute. The Prosecution is suggesting the following procedure: And before deciding, the Chamber must see what the reactions of the Defence are. The Prosecution quite rightly notes that videoconference testimony entails considerable cost. And if there's only one witness, it's not worth setting in motion this whole procedure and that the available witness would then testify on another day. But the solution that is suggested would be that nevertheless, we proceed notwithstanding the application to the Appeals Chamber. We proceed with the closed session testimony; and if the Appeals Chamber rules that there was no reason to grant protective measures, then the testimony itself would be made public. The Chamber would like to hear the reaction of Mr. Dixon and Mr. Bourgon after that. I hope you have understood the mechanism which is very subtle and which has been suggested by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would not at this stage agree to that mechanism for two reasons: The first being that as I indicated earlier, Your Honour, this witness, when he came here before Your Honours, made it absolutely clear that if he was not granted protective measures, he would not be in a position to be able to testify. Whether he's entitled to say that or not and what the consequences of that are is a different matter. But he said that he would not be able to because of the position he held in his church and the instructions that he had been given by his church. And it's for that reason primarily that it would need to be resolved before he testifies. And then second, Your Honour, there's the question of the right to a public hearing, which in our view must mean that the public are able to have access to that testimony as it is being given. Whether that be on the internet or here in the courtroom as opposed to only being able to read a transcript much later on. The effect of that is in our view quite significantly diminished. So our submission would be that the matter has to be resolved first. Otherwise, the witness will be in a position where he is testifying and he won't know whether or not that might be made public later and then it's going to be dependent on a decision which is still to come. And in our view it should be resolved first. If it means that the other videolink witness must wait and the two are done together at a later stage in June in order to save money, that would seem to be a prudent action. Not to have either videolink witness now, but to wait until after the decision, and then to have both at that stage, depending on what the decision is. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Simply to tell the Chamber that we support the arguments set forth by the Defence of Mr. Kubura. And there's an additional factor: And that is that the witness can only testify for 30 minutes a day, and maybe in a week or two, his condition will be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will turn now to the issue for which I initially asked to address Your Honours. Pursuant to the Trial Chamber's oral order of 17 May 2004, the Prosecution was ordered to provide a number of items for the Trial Chamber. As Your Honours are aware, earlier this week, in order to clarify some of those issues and to provide updates to the Trial Chamber with respect to progress, the Chamber's legal officer, Ms. Godart, met with senior trial attorney Mr. Withopf, and I believe an analyst from the Prosecution team, and the investigative team leader was also present at that meeting. Earlier this week, before her departure, Ms. Godart called me and informed me that I was to set forth on the record a description of what happened at that meeting and also progress with respect to the Prosecution's efforts to fulfil the terms of the Trial Chamber's oral order. I'm relying primarily, Mr. President, on both information provided by Mr. Withopf as well as from a number of other team members who have been tasked with performing these duties. Let me begin going category by category through the issues as set forth in the oral order of 17 May. Category A, number 1, related to information on documents provided by governments to the Office of the Prosecutor, either on their own accord or in response to requests submitted to them by the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. President, Your Honours, it does not appear to be possible to link all of the documents to specific requests for assistance or what we know as RFAs that were sent to the governments in question. Many of the documents we can link to such requests; however, as Your Honours may be aware, requests for assistance are sent by a number of Prosecution teams involving a number of different trials and investigations. As a result of some of those requests for assistance, information comes into the hands of the Office of the Prosecutor which when we then electronically search. That information may have been provided to a different team pursuant to different requests but which we are not able always to specifically track. We have an internal tracking system that's known as the information index form, which is a form that is completed at the time we receive each and every document. A single form is produced and created every time the Office of the Prosecutor receives a document. Some of these IIFs or information index forms do not provide enough specific information for us to track which request for assistance the document was a response to. Again, some of them -- this is only a smaller number of documents. Most of the documents we are in a position to track how -- or in response to which request for assistance the specific document came from. And I have the team leader currently working on this as part of an overall affidavit, if you will, or statement. And as I've previously indicated, we will be seeking leave to add him to our witness list during the month of June to explain, among other things, this very subject matter to Your Honours. The second category or second item under category A concerns the Trial Chamber's requests that archivists be called. Mr. President, as I previously indicated, Mrs. Benjamin will in fact be in Sarajevo and Zenica next week speaking to the archivists. I should also indicate that -- two things in this respect: Of course, we are dependent to a certain extent upon the Bosnian government to identify the specific archivists. I should also indicate in this regard that the archivists who she will be speaking are not necessarily the same people whose names appear on some of the receipts for documents that were seized or taken from the archives. The simple reason for that, Mr. President, is that when the investigators went into the archives to take documents, they were often accompanied not by the archivists themselves, but by individuals designated by the archivists or by the Bosnian liaison officers assisting and accompanying our investigators as they conducted their searches. So the archivists may or may not be the same people whose names you might see on receipts. But we will take care of all of that in terms of the testimony of the archivists. 22 I should also state, Mr. President, in this respect that although I had previously indicated that we might seek leave to call this evidence through Rule 92 bis, that is not the case. We will not do that. We will bring those archivists here to The Hague to testify about the archives. As I indicated yesterday, it is unlikely that those witnesses, however, would be available during the week of the 7th of June and leaving us with a potential gap of any witnesses during that week. With respect to the third item under category A, information relating to material in the possession of the Prosecution that would indicate whether specific documents were actually sent and received, as was explained to Mrs. Godart, in many instances the documents themselves indicate through -- by way of stamps or other markings on the documents whether they were -- whether the documents were actually sent or received. In addition, a sequential analysis may be of great assistance in that respect, and we are currently undertaking such an analysis and will provide that information to the Trial Chamber as quickly as possible. That, however, given the large number of documents and the fact that many of these tasks must be done by the same small group of people who are familiar with the documents means that this information might not be available to the Trial Chamber for several weeks. With respect to item 4, calling a former high-ranking member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to testify about the drafting of orders, the Office of the Prosecution is in the process of identifying specific individuals who would be able to provide the Trial Chamber with this information. Again, pursuant to the protocols that are in place, if those individuals are currently still serving in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we are required to request certain steps be taken by the Bosnian government and their permission for us to approach these individuals. Again, this process could result in a delay of several weeks in order to obtain the necessary permission from the Bosnian government and/or even assistance in locating where these witnesses might be, and then allowing us to interview them, make the information available, et cetera. With respect to samples of the accuseds' signatures, we will provide the Trial Chamber with two packets of information with documents that were signed by the accused. In the event the Trial Chamber requires or needs an expert witness to assist in any type of handwriting analysis, we will endeavour to assist Your Honours in locating such an individual to make a comparison, if that is required. With respect to the origin of documents, my understanding was that Mr. Withopf explained to Ms. Godart that as a general rule when we seize or receive documents from governments, there is as a general rule no clear indication from the governments as to how they got the documents; that is, when we take copies of documents from the archives in Sarajevo, that archive does not tell us specifically where the documents came from. Again, I think the archivists may be able to shed some light on this item for the benefit of the Chamber. With respect to the operational logs and war diaries that were the subject of several periodic discussions, the total length of the respective logs and diaries runs to 1.369 pages. About 50 per cent of that material has been translated into a first-draft or first-draft translation in English. We are -- we have made requests for the remaining material to be translated into English and for revisions to be made to the pages which have previously been translated. This obviously will take a significant period of time to render full translations of these 1.369 pages. It is -- I hesitate to add potentially a very difficult task due to the fact that they are handwritten logs and many entries on some pages are illegible. With respect to category B and the first item listed thereunder, the Prosecution was ordered to provide a list of witnesses who could authenticate all of the documents. Based on discussions with members of the analytical and investigative team assigned to this case, the best we can do in that respect, Mr. President, is to provide that information by Friday, the 11th of June. The team is working on these documents, document by document. We have three staff members working full time on this task. But again, we do not anticipate that we could provide that information until Friday, June 11th. With respect to translations and missing translations, item 2 under category B, based on a memorandum provided by the Trial Chamber's legal officer with respect to missing documents, I can report that there were 52 draft translations listed on that memo. 26 of those 52 we have requested final translations. And 26 of those listed, it appears to us the final translations are available and we are determining whether or not those were actually included in any of the binders or other material previously provided. With respect to, again, a strict examination of missing documents, we are working on that. I also note that part of that order concerned annexes to documents. A number of the annexes are not in the possession of the Prosecution. So we have a document which refers to annexes, but in many instances we simply do not have the annexes referred to in the primary document. With respect to the videotapes, let me briefly say that if we are asked to provide or to view videotapes next week, we will certainly compile a sampling of those videotapes. And obviously, pare down the total amount of material that is included on the videotapes. But we would be in a position to show certain selected excerpts of those videotapes next week if that's what the Trial Chamber would like, in light of the fact that we may not have sufficient witnesses. Concerning telephone intercepts, I anticipate that middle of next week in light of the holiday on Monday, by the middle of next week, I will be able to provide full information on the telephone intercepts, where that material came from, et cetera. Concerning category C, and I'm almost finished, concerning category C, we were ordered to produce the witness Mika Tauro. Mr. Tauro is no longer with the Office of the Prosecutor, but he is available throughout the month of June. And again, we will call him at a time period when we have sufficient witnesses to kind of create a critical mass of witnesses, if you will. I don't anticipate his testimony to be very long at all. Simply pertaining to the charts and diagrams that he drew. With respect to the written order concerning another witness, we will file the documents the Chamber has requested by Wednesday of next week, which is the day 15 that we were asked to file certain documents and materials. And finally, item 3 under category C, the eight binders of noncontested documents and missing documents, again, we are working on that with a goal of completing it as quickly as possible. We have requested full English translations of those documents which were not included in those -- in that material. That is, Mr. President, my understanding of the meeting that took place earlier this week and the steps which we have taken in order to meet our obligation pursuant to the order. I do regret that these things could not have been completed quicker. I assure you that we are endeavouring to meet these deadlines as quickly as possible in order to bring the Prosecution case to a close as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll withdraw for a few minutes. Don't move because we have to render our decision on the matter of the videolink conference. As you know, it's a holiday on Monday, and there might be problems concerning plane tickets, et cetera. We'll deliberate about the matter immediately. It won't take long. --- Break taken at 1.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. As far as the videolink conference is concerned, the Trial Chamber has taken note of the comments made by the Prosecution and the Defence. And we hereby decide that the hearing of these two witnesses should be postponed. The Trial Chamber will inform you of the date next week. This means that the videolink conference scheduled for Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday will be cancelled. On the other hand, the Prosecution should broadcast the videos as we mentioned a while ago instead of having these witnesses heard by videolink. So this is the decision the Chamber has taken. And the Registrar can take all the necessary steps to cancel what was scheduled for next week. As far as the other issues raised by the Prosecution are concerned, as far as items A, B, and C are concerned, is there anything that Defence counsel would like to state at this point in time. Would the Defence would like to make any comments? The Prosecution has informed us of the work, of the stage of the work, of their work, and they referred to the oral decision of the 17th of May 2004. They are still engaged in their work, and the Prosecution will try to respect the order rendered. Nevertheless, they pointed out that certain difficulties had been encountered. Is there anything that the Defence would like to say? Yes, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we listened to what the Prosecution had to say. They have taken -- they are taking very serious steps in order to respect all the deadlines and to comply with the Trial Chamber's order. We have nothing we would like to state with regard to this issue, but we would like to be informed in time of the witnesses scheduled so that we can prepare for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And would the other Defence team like to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No observations at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will certainly make available both witness scheduling information as well as any new witness statements taken from any of the archivists or other witnesses as quickly as possible. If I could just seek clarification with respect to the videotapes, again, Mr. President, we clearly have a situation where with respect to the videotapes, I just want to be sure that my understanding is the same as the Chamber's.
