We will be prepared next week to show approximately 12 hours of videotape in those three days if that is what the Trial Chamber would like. We will -- with respect to those portions where there is audio also provide the transcripts of those videotapes. But again, we have time only in those three days to see about -- less than half. So we will with your leave be obviously selective in terms of what we are actually showing. And I simply want it to be clear, that unless you tell me otherwise, Mr. President, I will simply be in a position to show about 12 hours worth of videotapes with transcripts unless I'm ordered to do otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That was the sense of our decision. We think it would be appropriate to broadcast the videotapes. After they have been broadcast, if necessary, the parties can express their positions. The Prosecution and the Defence can state their positions, and then we will draw all the conclusions that can be drawn. You said that it would take 12 hours to broadcast -- to view these videos. That would mean four hours a day. The hearings only last for 4 hours and 45 minutes. So this is what we are in a position to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, again, Mr. President, I can make available six hours of excerpts or eight hours or ten hours or eleven and a half. It's -- I guess that's why I was seeking the guidance. I can make available as much or as little videotape as Your Honours might think. If you tell me you want to have six hours, then I will select what I think are the most relevant six hours out of the twenty-six hours of videotape we have available. If you tell me you want to see three hours, I'll do the same exercise. So, it's really up to Your Honours. Unless you want to see all of the videotapes, which we can't do next week anyway, I will make available as many hours of excerpts from the videotapes as Your Honours would like to see next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the videos are concerned, is there anything the Defence would like to state at this point in time? Because naturally, the Defence is not going to cross-examine the video. There is no one behind the video. So what is the Defence's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. At this point in time, Mr. President, we would like to know the following: We understand the procedure suggested by the Chamber would be to view the videos, and then engage in a debate. Mr. President, we have already made submissions to the effect that the videos require the presence of a witness in order to be able to authenticate the contents of the video, in order to authenticate what the video represents. If there is a videotape, we would like to know who is speaking, who wrote the text, and what the text represents. Without a witness, Mr. President, we believe that it would be very difficult to reach a decision concerning the admissibility into evidence of a video. And even if the images presented have great probative weight, nevertheless we would still have doubts about their reliability because we wouldn't know when the video was made, by whom, what the conditions were. We wouldn't know whether it's a collage, a written text, an interview. These are questions that would remain unanswered, Mr. President, after viewing the video. Naturally, if the viewing of the video would be part of a procedure leading to another stage which would involve getting other information via 92 bis statements, or via the author of the video. In such a case the circumstances would be different. But in this particular case, just viewing the video without having any access to any other support, it would be difficult for the Trial Chamber to rule on the admissibility of this evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Our understanding of this process is that there is a need to view the videos in order to assess the reliability or authenticity and the probative value to be given to the videos. And that Your Honours do require an opportunity to view the videos and for that to be done in public, and then thereafter to give the parties an opportunity to make submissions to Your Honour on whether the video should indeed be admitted in the first place. And we would, as Your Honours have indicated, make use of the opportunity to make submissions to Your Honours as to why in our view the videos should not be admitted. As Mr. Bourgon said, the first argument is of course a witness is required. But even if a witness is not required, in our view, the content of the videos is not of a sufficient nature to allow them to be admitted. But Your Honours have ordered that that process should take place in public. And that is our understanding of what will happen next week. And at the end of the process, Your Honours will be in a position to decide whether or not the videos should be admitted. And if so, or portions thereof, what weight will ultimately be attached to them. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will deliberate again. But for the moment, we are assuming that the videos will be broadcast next week. If by Tuesday we have taken a decision that will clarify the issue, we will inform you of our decision. Thank you. I would like to apologise to the interpreters for having worked a little longer than usual, and I will see everyone again on Tuesday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
